comparisons.peer_topic: Purpose and Scope of Corporation-wide Stress Testing
comparisons.peer_summary: The company conducts regular capital scenario management and stress forecasting to understand balance sheet, earnings, and capital sensitivities to a wide range of economic and business scenarios. These stress tests aim to develop a comprehensive understanding of potential impacts of on- and off-balance sheet risks to ensure financial resiliency and confidence among management, regulators, and investors.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and BAC disclose ongoing regulatory monitoring processes related to capital and risk management. JPM specifically highlights uncertainty in the finalization of GSIB surcharge and TLAC proposals, whereas BAC describes a broader, continuous capital scenario management and stress forecasting process to understand sensitivities to economic scenarios. While JPM focuses on the regulatory timeline uncertainty, BAC focuses on the internal analytical framework for assessing financial resiliency under various stress conditions.

sentences.text: Finalization of the above proposals, including the required implementation dates, is uncertain.
The Firm continues to monitor developments and potential impacts.

Integral to our Capital Planning, Financial Planning and Strategic Planning processes, we conduct capital scenario management and stress forecasting on a regular basis to better understand balance sheet, earnings and capital sensitivities to a wide range of economic and business scenarios, including economic and market conditions that are more severe than anticipated.

These stress forecasts provide an understanding of the potential impacts from our risk profile on the balance sheet, earnings and capital, and serve as a key component of our capital and risk management practices.

comparisons.peer_topic: TLAC and LTD Regulatory Requirements for U.S. GSIBs
comparisons.peer_summary: U.S. Global Systemically Important Banks (GSIBs) must maintain minimum levels of Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) and eligible Long-Term Debt (LTD) based on consolidated risk-weighted assets and total leverage exposure. The purpose of these requirements is to ensure the orderly resolution of these institutions under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act, with specific company amounts detailed in the Capital Resources section.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and Citi disclose requirements for U.S. Global Systemically Important Banks (GSIBs) regarding Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) and Long-Term Debt (LTD). JPM notes the uncertainty in the finalization of these specific proposals and implementation dates. Citi defines the requirement as maintaining minimum levels based on risk-weighted assets and total leverage exposure to ensure orderly resolution under Dodd-Frank. Both identify TLAC/LTD as a key regulatory obligation for GSIBs.

sentences.text: Finalization of the above proposals, including the required implementation dates, is uncertain.
U.S. GSIBs are required to maintain minimum levels of TLAC and eligible LTD, each set by reference to the GSIB's consolidated risk-weighted assets (RWA) and total leverage exposure.
The intended purpose of the requirements is to facilitate the orderly resolution of U.S. GSIBs under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act.

comparisons.peer_summary: Citi participates in financial industry and regulatory initiatives, including scenario analysis, to inform climate risk measurement and actively engages with regulators on climate and sustainable finance developments.

The similarity lies in the disclosure of an active monitoring stance toward evolving regulatory initiatives, though the specific subject matter (capital structure vs. climate risk) differs.

comparisons.peer_topic: TLAC and External Long-Term Debt Regulatory Requirements
comparisons.peer_summary: Regulatory requirements for TLAC to risk-weighted assets include an 18% minimum, a 2.5% buffer, a zero countercyclical capital buffer, and a 1.5% G-SIB surcharge, while TLAC to leverage exposure includes a 7.5% minimum and a 2.0% buffer.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and Goldman Sachs discuss the components of TLAC requirements for GSIBs, including the G-SIB surcharge. JPM highlights the uncertainty surrounding the finalization and implementation of these proposals. Goldman Sachs provides the specific regulatory calculation details, noting the TLAC to RWA requirement includes a 1.5% G-SIB surcharge. Both companies confirm the existence of a G-SIB surcharge within the TLAC framework.

sentences.text: Finalization of the above proposals, including the required implementation dates, is uncertain.

• The TLAC to RWAs requirement included (i) the 18% minimum, (ii) the 2.5% buffer, (iii) the countercyclical capital buffer, which the FRB has set to zero percent and (iv) the 1.5% G-SIB surcharge (Method 1).

comparisons.peer_topic: Basel III and G-SIB Surcharge Monitoring
comparisons.peer_summary: U.S. banking agencies proposed revisions to risk-based capital standards (Basel III Endgame Proposal) on July 27, 2023, and the company continues to monitor this rulemaking along with proposed revisions to the G-SIB capital surcharge framework.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and Morgan Stanley disclose monitoring of regulatory proposals affecting GSIB capital standards, specifically mentioning the G-SIB surcharge. JPM notes the uncertainty in the finalization of GSIB surcharge and TLAC proposals. Morgan Stanley explicitly states it continues to monitor proposed revisions to the G-SIB capital surcharge framework alongside the Basel III Endgame Proposal. Both firms are actively tracking changes to the G-SIB surcharge mechanism.

comparisons.peer_topic: TLAC and LTD Ratio Definitions and Requirements
comparisons.peer_summary: Required TLAC ratios include applicable buffers and consist of CET1 capital, Additional Tier 1 capital (excluding noncontrolling interests), and eligible LTD, with LTD reduced by 50% for unpaid principal due in one to two years. Clean holding company requirements prohibit covered BHCs from incurring external debt with maturities less than one year and cap certain other external liabilities at 5% of outstanding external TLAC, while capital deductions apply for investments in unsecured debt instruments issued by the Parent Company or other G-SIBs.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and Morgan Stanley address TLAC and eligible LTD requirements for GSIBs. JPM focuses on the uncertainty of the regulatory proposal finalization and implementation dates. Morgan Stanley details the composition of External TLAC, including CET1, Additional Tier 1, and eligible LTD, and notes clean holding company requirements prohibiting short-term external debt. While JPM discusses the regulatory timeline, Morgan Stanley defines the structural components of the requirement.
